title: Strategy Is Choice
hook: Six growth priorities, each one plausible. None of them knows what the others are doing.
counterintuition: The more goals you add to a strategic plan, the weaker the plan becomes. Not because focus is virtuous in itself, but because each goal that requires different customers, a different field, or different capabilities breaks the internal logic that makes strategy work. A list of intentions is not a cascade.
tryThisNow: Pull out any active plan you have. Pick the second-biggest priority and ask whether it requires different customers or capabilities than the first. A conflict there is where the cascade breaks.
keyTakeaway: A strategy only exists when five choices cohere: aspiration, field, advantage, capabilities, and systems all pointing in the same direction. A thorough list of priorities is not yet a strategy.

breakdown.fastRead:
Kate put three growth goals on the bakery whiteboard Thursday morning: wholesale accounts, a subscription box, and a second location by spring. Each one made sense. None of them pointed at the same wall.

She was not planning badly. She was planning well while skipping strategy.

Strategy is not a list of good ideas. It is a cascade of five choices that must cohere: what winning looks like, where you compete, how you beat alternatives there, what capabilities that requires, and what systems keep all of it reinforced. When the choices do not fit, the list is a wish.

Kate needed a choice, not a longer whiteboard.
breakdown.deepRead:
The cascade starts with what you are actually trying to win. Not a growth target. Not a vision statement. A specific choice about which customers you want to delight and which alternatives you intend to beat them on.

That first choice immediately shapes the second: where you will and will not compete, across geography, customer segment, channel, and category. The second shapes the third: what kind of advantage or value equation will beat the alternatives in that specific field. Capabilities come next, but not as a talent inventory. They are the specific things your organization must be able to do to deliver the how-to-win choice. The fifth choice is management systems: the reviews, measures, and accountability routines that reinforce all four prior choices. A strategy is not complete until all five are made and all five fit.

Olay did not recover because P&G invested harder in what the brand already was. It recovered because the choices fit: a clearer target customer, a sharper price position, a more attractive market segment, and capabilities that could deliver the new offer all pointed in the same direction at once. Changing any one of those choices would have pulled the others out of alignment.

That is the coherence test. Pick any choice in your current strategy document and ask: if I changed this, would it require me to change the others? If the answer is no, the choices are not connected. They are parallel aspirations sharing a page.

Now try it on your own priorities. Pick the second one. Ask whether it requires different customers than the first, a different field, or a different set of capabilities. A conflict there is where the cascade breaks.

A list of priorities, however ambitious, is not a strategy until the choices reinforce each other.
breakdown.fullRead:
A consulting partner opens the week with six new proposals in six different sectors: healthcare technology, environmental compliance, supply-chain logistics, public-sector procurement, commercial real estate advisory, and one more. Every proposal looks winnable. Every one requires a different set of client credentials, a different delivery model, and subject matter expertise the practice does not currently have.

He calls this a strong pipeline. There is no strategy here.

The difference becomes visible in what accumulates. A practice that wins in six sectors earns six one-time engagements. It does not earn the deep pattern-recognition in any single field that makes the next engagement there faster to win, cheaper to deliver, and more credible in the client's eyes. Each new sector is a restart from zero. The pipeline grows. The capability stands still.

A coherent where-to-play choice creates the opposite dynamic. Each engagement in the chosen field builds on the last. The referral network tightens. The practice develops the case examples, the regulatory familiarity, and the judgment that a generalist cannot replicate. That advantage compresses over time. It is only available to organizations that made a choice about where to compete.

Take a nonprofit that started with a clear workforce development mission and grew to nine programs in four years, each one added because a grant came through. Early childhood literacy. Emergency food assistance. Digital skills for adults. Housing navigation. Each one good at something. Together, they became a grant management company operating under a workforce banner. When the largest funder asked what the organization was best at, the honest answer was: whichever program the last check was written for.

A strategy is not what you say you are doing. A strategy is what the coherence of your choices reveals you are actually committed to.

The coherence test asks one question for every choice in the cascade: if I changed this, would it require me to change the others? If yes, the choices are connected. If no, they are a list.

Run the test on a typical planning document and most priorities survive the swap. The digital transformation initiative can be removed without changing the customer experience initiative. The talent program can be modified without touching the revenue target. Each one is a parallel track on its own trajectory. They share a page. They do not share a logic.

Now try it on your own work. Take the third priority you are currently running and ask: if I stopped it tomorrow, would anything else I am doing change? If the answer is no, that priority is not part of your strategy. It is a separate project running alongside it.

A software team once built infrastructure for three customer segments simultaneously. Every architecture decision optimized for one segment was challenged by advocates for the other two and resolved with a compromise that slightly served each while fully serving none. The product shipped. Users in all three segments were moderately satisfied. The team was exhausted by negotiations that had no resolution principle because the strategic choice at the top of the cascade was never made.

The cascade does not care how hard the team works. It cares whether the choices cohere.

Olay's recovery is the clean version. The choices pointed in the same direction: one customer type, one market position, one advantage logic, one capability system built to deliver it. Once those choices fit, every subsequent decision had a resolution principle. The product team knew who they were building for. The pricing team knew what position to hold. Execution became faster and less contentious because the cascade had already resolved most of the arguments.

That is what a coherent strategy gives you. Not a guarantee of winning. A resolution principle for trade-offs. And trade-offs arrive every day, at every level, whether or not you have named your cascade.

Name the cascade. Then check whether it coheres. That is where strategy begins.

examples.title: Claire Counts What Three Goals Actually Require

planSpec.domain: artisan bakery deciding between wholesale accounts and a direct-to-consumer subscription model
planSpec.audience: a small-business owner who has written down three growth goals but cannot decide which way to invest
planSpec.stakes: investing in the wrong channel depletes cash before the busy season and leaves both paths half-built
planSpec.requiredBeat: the owner lists the three growth goals and realizes that each goal requires a different capability and customer relationship: the three cannot be pursued at once without none of them cohering

examples.scenario: 'Can we add a fourth tier?' the line cook calls at 7:50 a.m. Claire is at the bakery counter with a wholesale proposal, flour still on her apron. Three goals are on the whiteboard: more wholesale accounts, a subscription box, a second location by spring. Wholesale needs a delivery van and a sales rep. The box needs a packing station. The location needs a manager and six months of cash. None of the three overlap. She must decide before the flour delivery at nine which goal gets this month's reinvestment.
examples.whatToDo: Name which of the three goals fits the bakery's current capability (delivery, packaging, or a second kitchen) and fund only that one. The other two go on hold until the cascade from the first choice is stable.
examples.whyItMatters: Three growth goals each requiring different customers, capabilities, and capital are three separate strategies. Pursuing all three simultaneously means none of them gets enough resources to cohere.

examples.title: Thomas Sees What the Program List Became

planSpec.domain: a nonprofit choosing between expanding grant-funded program breadth and deepening a single program's outcomes
planSpec.audience: an executive director facing a board that wants growth and funders who want depth
planSpec.stakes: if the org tries to grow program count and deepen impact simultaneously, neither goal will be achieved and the largest funder may walk
planSpec.requiredBeat: the director sees that every program added in the last two years was chased because of a grant opportunity, not because it fit the org's stated aspiration; the wish list grew while the actual strategy dissolved

examples.scenario: It took Thomas three budget cycles to notice the pattern. The nonprofit had added six programs in four years, each one triggered by a grant opportunity, not a strategic choice. The list had grown from three programs to nine, each serving a different population under a different theory of change. He has an annual impact report due in a week and must decide whether to present all nine programs as a coherent portfolio or acknowledge, for the first time, that the cascade has dissolved into funder management.
examples.whatToDo: Before writing the impact report, trace each program back to the original aspiration. Any program whose origin was a grant opportunity rather than the stated mission signals that the cascade needs to be rebuilt.
examples.whyItMatters: A portfolio shaped by incoming grants has replaced the strategic cascade with a set of funder priorities. The impact report cannot fix that, but naming it honestly is the first step toward building a coherent field choice.

examples.title: Etienne's Pipeline Has Six Proposals and No Strategy

planSpec.domain: a management consulting practice choosing which client industries to serve
planSpec.audience: a partner-level consultant who wants to grow revenue but has taken on projects in six different sectors
planSpec.stakes: the practice cannot build a repeatable capability in any sector if it keeps dispersing into new ones
planSpec.requiredBeat: the consultant lays out a pipeline of six potential new engagements in six different industries and recognizes that every proposal requires credentials the practice does not have. The cascade question forces a choice about which field to own

examples.scenario: At 9:14 a.m. Monday, Etienne opens a shared drive with six new proposals in six different sectors. Each one was won on a different partner's personal relationship with a new industry client. He must decide before the two o'clock pipeline review which sectors to pursue and which to cut. The practice has never lost a proposal. It has also never built repeatable capability in any single sector. Every engagement is a restart from scratch.
examples.whatToDo: Pick the one or two sectors where the practice's existing delivery record creates a real edge over generalists. Decline proposals that require building credentials from zero until the first sector choice is stable.
examples.whyItMatters: Six sectors means six fresh starts. Revenue grows but capability stays flat. Without a coherent field choice, the practice cannot build the pattern-recognition that makes each next engagement faster to win and stronger to deliver.

examples.title: Luca Asks Which Listener the Station Is Winning

planSpec.domain: a community radio station choosing between a hyper-local news format and a broad music and talk format
planSpec.audience: a board and programming director deciding where the station's scarce production capacity should go
planSpec.stakes: the station's current format serves no audience especially well, and digital competitors have already taken the casual listener
planSpec.requiredBeat: the programming director asks the board which listeners they are actually trying to serve: the question exposes that the current format was inherited, not chosen, and that no capabilities support either potential direction

examples.scenario: Which listener is the station trying to win: the one who left for a podcast three years ago or the one who never found the station? Luca brings the question to the programming committee predicting quick consensus. After sixty minutes of debate, no one agrees. He realizes the current split format is not a programming choice. It is the documented result of a strategic decision that was never made.
examples.whatToDo: Name which listener type the station is competing for in the next eighteen months. Every scheduling, staffing, and production decision should follow from that one choice, not be made independently of it.
examples.whyItMatters: A format serving two incompatible audiences with one production budget serves neither well. Without naming which listener the station is competing to win, every quarterly format review restarts the same argument from zero.

examples.title: Hadiya Sees What the Job Description Actually Says

planSpec.domain: an academic department deciding whether to compete for graduate student rankings or deepen undergraduate teaching quality
planSpec.audience: a department chair who has received budget for a new hire and must decide what kind of position to fill
planSpec.stakes: the hire will either reinforce a research identity or a teaching identity; the two paths require different capabilities and different measures of success
planSpec.requiredBeat: the chair realizes the job description trying to attract both a researcher and a teacher is a symptom of a missing strategic choice, not a creative solution to it

examples.scenario: The department conference room at 4:15 p.m. on a Tuesday in March: one hire budget, two printed job descriptions, twelve criteria total. Before: Hadiya submits the description with six research-aligned criteria and six teaching-aligned criteria, hoping to attract a candidate who can do both. After: the shortlist produces candidates mediocre in both directions, and she sees that the description was a symptom of a strategic choice the department had never made.
examples.whatToDo: Choose which aspiration drives the hire: graduate ranking or undergraduate quality: rewrite the description from that choice alone. Criteria pointing two directions attract candidates who fit neither.
examples.whyItMatters: A job description split between two aspirations signals the underlying strategic choice was never made. The resulting hire partially serves both directions and fully serves neither.

examples.title: James Traces Three Years of Reactive Inventory

planSpec.domain: a regional hardware retailer deciding whether to compete on product selection breadth or on contractor-service relationships
planSpec.audience: a second-generation owner whose store has been caught between a big-box home-improvement chain and a specialty supplier
planSpec.stakes: the store cannot match the big-box on price and selection and cannot match the specialist on depth; the current position wins on nothing
planSpec.requiredBeat: the owner traces the last three years of inventory decisions and realizes each one was reactive to a competitor move, not advancing a coherent identity for any specific customer

examples.scenario: Twelve pallets of slow-moving inventory fill the storeroom, each bought in the last three years to match a competitor's promotion. James has run the hardware store for eleven years. He traces the inventory purchase by purchase and finds that every decision was reactive: matching a competitor's move and not advancing a coherent position for any customer type. The store stocked for everyone and has loyalty from no one.
examples.whatToDo: Name the one customer type the store's location, staff knowledge, and relationship capacity could serve better than any competitor in the area. Stop carrying inventory optimized for the other types.
examples.whyItMatters: Stocking for every customer means competing against the chain's selection and the specialist's depth simultaneously. That position wins nothing. Coherent field choice means the inventory, staff, and service all point at the same customer.

questions.prompt: A company has a vision statement, a growth target, a prioritized list of twelve initiatives, and a detailed 90-day execution plan. The leadership team is proud of the document's rigor. Which element, taken alone, constitutes a strategy?
choices: None of them; a strategy requires five mutually reinforcing choices, not any single element.
The growth target, because it names what the company is trying to achieve.
The 90-day plan, because it shows what the company will actually do.
questions.explanation: A strategy requires five reinforcing choices. A growth target is an aspiration, a plan is an execution schedule, and an initiatives list is a set of priorities. None becomes strategy until all five choices cohere around a specific field, advantage, capability system, and management logic.

questions.prompt: A boutique hotel was known as a quiet weekend retreat for couples. This year it added conference facilities, a rooftop restaurant, and a pet-friendly floor, each responding to a different customer type's demand. Which move would most strengthen its strategy?
choices: Accept all three additions because each individually improves revenue.
Identify which addition best fits the original positioning and invest only in that one.
Hire a larger marketing team to promote all three new offerings simultaneously.
questions.explanation: The hotel's original positioning as a couples retreat defines one customer. Each addition targeting a different customer type breaks the cascade. Testing each addition against the original aspiration before committing keeps the five choices coherent and prevents the offer from drifting toward everyone.

questions.prompt: A law firm's new strategic plan lists twelve priorities: digital modernization, international expansion, three new practice areas, a new branch office, and a client diversity initiative. Each priority was added because a different partner championed it. How should the leadership team evaluate this document?
choices: Approve it; twelve priorities show breadth and strategic ambition.
Rank the priorities by projected revenue and cut to the top five.
Test whether the twelve choices cohere: whether each choice enables and constrains the others.
questions.explanation: Cutting by revenue is execution triage, not strategy. The coherence test asks whether removing any choice would weaken the others. A list where each priority can be swapped without affecting the rest has no shared logic and is not yet a strategy, just a collection of partners' preferences.

questions.prompt: A software product serves enterprise clients who need security and dedicated support, and consumer users who need simplicity and low price. The team is scoping a new authentication feature. What strategic question should they ask first?
choices: Which customer type does this feature most reinforce, and is that the customer the strategy is built around?
Which customer type represents the larger addressable market?
Which customer type pays a higher price per seat?
questions.explanation: Market size and seat revenue are financial metrics, not strategic ones. The strategic question is whether the feature reinforces the chosen customer and advantage. Building for two incompatible customer types prevents the capability system from pointing in one direction and weakens both simultaneously.

questions.prompt: A nonprofit's program list grew from three to nine in four years. Each new program was triggered by an incoming grant from a different funder, not by the organization's stated aspiration. A major funder is now asking for an impact summary. What does this growth pattern reveal about the organization's strategy?
choices: The nonprofit has a strong opportunistic culture and is funding its growth effectively.
The five-choice cascade has collapsed: the portfolio is shaped by funder priorities, not by a coherent aspiration and field choice.
The nonprofit needs a better fundraising strategy to reduce its dependence on grants.
questions.explanation: Grant-driven program addition substitutes funder agendas for the organization's own cascade. Growth without a coherent aspiration and field choice produces a portfolio where programs compete for staff and resources instead of building on each other toward a single winning position.

questions.prompt: A consulting practice wins engagements in six different sectors each year, each win anchored to one partner's personal relationship with a client in that sector. The practice has not built expertise depth in any single field for three years. What is the primary strategic failure?
choices: The practice is dangerously dependent on individual partners for all its revenue.
The practice needs a stronger marketing function to attract clients without personal relationships.
There is no coherent where-to-play choice, so no capability or credential can accumulate in any sector.
questions.explanation: Partner dependency is a talent risk, not the strategic failure here. Without a chosen field, every engagement is a restart in unfamiliar territory. A practice that builds no sector depth cannot develop the pattern-recognition, case examples, or referral network that would make the next engagement there faster, stronger, or cheaper.

questions.prompt: A manager tests her company's five strategic priorities with the coherence question and finds that each priority could be changed or removed without requiring any changes to the others. What does this test reveal?
choices: The five priorities lack internal logic; they are parallel tracks sharing a document, not a strategy cascade.
The strategy is well-designed; independent priorities allow the company to adapt faster to changing conditions.
The manager should add more priorities to create stronger connections between the existing ones.
questions.explanation: Independent priorities with no mutual dependence form a list. A real cascade means each choice constrains and enables the others. Five priorities that can each be swapped without disturbing the rest give the organization no resolution principle when trade-offs appear; every conflict is litigated from scratch.

questions.prompt: A department must choose between growing graduate rankings through research hires or deepening undergraduate quality through pedagogy hires. The chair proposes hiring one candidate who has both a strong research record and strong teaching evaluations. What is the main strategic problem with this solution?
choices: A candidate with both strengths will cost too much for the department's budget.
Such a dual-strength candidate is unlikely to be found in the current market.
The hybrid hire defers the strategic choice and produces a result that partially serves two directions rather than fully advancing either.
questions.explanation: The hybrid hire feels like a creative solution but avoids the cascade decision. Choosing between graduate ranking and undergraduate quality requires commitment because the capabilities, measures, and downstream resource allocations for each direction differ. A hire serving both ends reinforces neither, and the cascade remains unresolved after the hire.

questions.prompt: A regional bakery owner has three growth goals: more wholesale accounts, a monthly subscription box, and a second location. Each requires different equipment, staff, and customer relationships. She has enough cash and attention for one goal this year. What is the right strategic move?
choices: Pursue all three at reduced investment to test which one gains traction first.
Pick the goal whose capability requirements best fit the bakery's current activity system and the field it wants to own.
Choose the goal with the highest projected revenue for the next twelve months.
questions.explanation: Revenue projection tests financial attractiveness, not strategic fit. The three goals are structurally different businesses in terms of customer, capability, and channel. Funding the one that fits the current activity system creates a coherent foundation. Spreading across all three produces partial infrastructure for each and strategic advantage in none.

reviewCards.front: Your plan has five bold priorities and none of them require the team to stop doing anything. What does that tell you?
reviewCards.back: It signals the priorities are not yet a strategy. A real cascade requires choices that constrain each other: when you add one, the others limit it. A list where everything can coexist without conflict has no internal logic.

reviewCards.front: What are the five choices in a strategy cascade?
reviewCards.back: Winning aspiration, where to play, how to win, the required capabilities, and management systems; each one enabling and constraining the others. A strategy is only complete when all five cohere.

reviewCards.front: A consulting practice wins in a new sector every quarter but builds no reputation in any of them. What strategic choice is missing?
reviewCards.back: A where-to-play choice. Without naming which field to compete in, each engagement is a restart from zero. No capability, credential, or referral network accumulates to create an advantage that compounds over time.

reviewCards.front: What is the coherence test for a strategy?
reviewCards.back: Ask whether changing any one choice would require you to change the others. If the choices can each be swapped independently without disturbing the rest, they are not connected; you have a list, not a cascade.

reviewCards.front: What made the Olay turnaround work strategically?
reviewCards.back: The choices fit each other: a clearer target customer, a sharper price position, a more attractive market segment, and capabilities that could deliver the new offer all pointed in the same direction. Coherence, not increased investment in the existing approach.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: You learn to distinguish a strategy cascade from a list of priorities by testing whether the choices reinforce each other. You practice the coherence test: asking whether each choice in a plan would require changing the others if it were modified. A plan passes when the choices constrain each other. A list fails when each priority can be swapped without disturbing the rest.

ifThenPlans.context: reviewing a business or team plan
ifThenPlans.plan: If any priority in the plan could be removed or swapped without requiring changes to the others, name the coherence gap before approving the document.

If the new opportunity requires a different customer, field, or capability than the current strategy, treat it as a second strategy and evaluate it on its own terms, not added to the existing cascade.

ifThenPlans.context: evaluating a growth proposal with multiple goals
ifThenPlans.plan: If the proposal lists goals that each require different customers and capabilities, decide which one fits the current cascade before committing resources to any of them.
If a hire or budget allocation is being justified by two incompatible strategic aspirations simultaneously, the underlying cascade choice has not been made; resolve the cascade first.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Find one project or initiative you are currently running. Trace it backward through the cascade: does it require a specific field choice, a specific advantage logic, specific capabilities, and specific reinforcing systems? Name any link in the chain that is missing or vague. That gap is where your strategy currently stops.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each week, take one team decision you made and ask whether it reinforced a coherent cascade or implicitly started a parallel one. If it started a parallel one, name that explicitly and decide whether the strategy should shift toward it or the decision should be reversed.

memorableLines.text: She was not planning badly. She was planning well while skipping strategy.
memorableLines.why: The two-beat sentence names the trap precisely: good process, wrong level of thinking.

memorableLines.text: A strategy is not what you say you are doing. A strategy is what the coherence of your choices reveals you are actually committed to.
memorableLines.why: The pivot from declaration to evidence surfaces the gap between stated aspiration and actual portfolio.

memorableLines.text: Name the cascade. Then check whether it coheres. That is where strategy begins.
memorableLines.why: Three short imperatives compress the whole chapter's lesson into a sequence the reader can run right now.
